anchor: Collectively, these experiments establish the compatibility of the microfluidic platform with primary cortical neuronal culture, compartment-specific axonal labeling, and automated quantitative imaging. Further experiments using independent neuronal preparations will be required to determine biological reproducibility across cultures.
text: Culture, labeling and imaging compatibility are already reported, together with the single-preparation limit. Repeating that limit here adds no new result; the separate biological experiments are discussed with the hydrogel paper.

anchor: The hybrid fabrication strategy developed in this study provides a scalable approach for producing compartmentalized microfluidic culture devices by integrating photolithographically defined microfeatures with 3D-printed, millimeter-scale structures on reusable silicon-wafer molds. Building on previous advances in multiscale molding and the elimination of manual reservoir punching, our approach introduces a coordinated parametric design framework that enables the simultaneous alignment and attachment of large arrays of well-forming inserts to patterned wafers. This strategy addresses a practical limitation of conventional PDMS microfluidic fabrication, in which high-resolution microchannels can be reproduced by soft lithography, but the formation of individual culture wells frequently requires additional processing after casting. By incorporating all well-forming structures into a reusable mold, the method separates the specialized fabrication steps required to construct the mold from subsequent production of complete microfluidic devices. The resulting platform combines customizable microfluidic geometries with a standardized plate format suitable for medium-throughput biological experimentation.
text: Ristola combines SU-8 features with printed well-forming inserts, making it the direct comparison for our alignment method. Starting there brings out the added step: aligning and bonding the whole array together. The deleted opening repeats the Introduction.

anchor: The combination of photolithography and resin printing also exploits the complementary capabilities of these fabrication technologies. Photolithography remains well suited to defining micrometer-scale structures, whereas resin printing provides an accessible means of producing larger three-dimensional features. Recent developments in printed molds and hybrid fabrication have expanded the range of structures that can be manufactured for biological microfluidic applications, although achievable resolution, PDMS curing compatibility, and surface treatment remain important considerations (PMIDs: 40190179; 40667579).
text: Repeating these fabrication-scale comparisons restarts the Introduction's background. This paragraph instead needs to explain why the resin stays in the mold rather than in the culture device.
